session: Session 8: Distributed Databases and the CAP Theorem

questions.question: What limitation of the single-node PostgreSQL setup motivates distributed databases in the lecture?

options.A: Single nodes cannot enforce ACID properties.
options.B: Hardware failure or excessive demand can disrupt the whole service.
options.C: A single instance cannot create B-Tree indexes.
options.D: Single-node databases cannot store AI features.

questions.explanation: The recap raises SSD failure and one million simultaneous requests as single-machine risks.

questions.question: A team adds CPU cores and RAM to its existing database server without introducing other nodes. Which strategy is this?

options.A: Horizontal scaling
options.D: Read replication

questions.explanation: Scale-up adds resources to an existing server rather than adding servers.

questions.question: Which combination is identified as a drawback of vertical scaling?

options.A: Hardware ceiling and a remaining single point of failure
options.C: Replica lag and replica read-only errors
options.D: Complex routing among hundreds of nodes

questions.explanation: Scale-up faces physical hardware limits and does not eliminate the single point of failure.

questions.question: Which change best illustrates horizontal scaling?

options.A: Replacing a disk with a larger SSD
options.D: Adding standard servers that operate as one logical service

questions.explanation: Scale-out connects multiple commodity servers to act as a logical unit.

questions.question: Which benefit of horizontal scaling is especially relevant when one server unexpectedly fails?

options.A: All requests must wait for the failed node to recover.
options.B: Other nodes can continue serving the workload.
options.D: The system no longer requires network communication.

questions.explanation: The lecture associates scale-out with high availability through multiple nodes.

questions.question: A single-server service goes offline whenever its operating system must reboot for security patches. Which problem does this illustrate?

options.A: A hash collision
options.D: Eventual consistency

questions.explanation: A single node creates maintenance downtime as well as hardware and software failure exposure.

questions.question: Compared with scale-up, what additional operational cost is emphasized for scale-out?

options.A: Increased network and coordination complexity
options.B: A strict limit imposed by one motherboard
options.C: An inability to use inexpensive servers
options.D: The need to store everything on one disk

questions.explanation: The comparison table notes that horizontal scaling has greater complexity because of network overhead.

questions.question: In database replication, what is copied between servers?

options.A: Only SQL execution plans
options.D: Copies of database information maintained on different machines

questions.explanation: Replication maintains multiple copies of data on different physical servers.

questions.question: Which pair of objectives motivates replication in the slides?

options.A: Removing all indexes and eliminating transactions
options.B: Improving fault tolerance and read performance
options.C: Avoiding schemas and preventing any network failure
options.D: Reducing database size through horizontal partitioning

questions.explanation: The lecture lists reliability/fault tolerance and read performance as motivations.

questions.question: In the primary-replica model presented, which node normally accepts INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE?

options.A: The primary
options.D: A dedicated backup server disconnected from the cluster

questions.explanation: The primary is the write-capable source of truth; replicas serve reads and synchronize.

questions.question: What role do replicas play in the lecture’s primary-replica architecture?

options.A: Assign unique subsets of user IDs
options.C: Serve reads and synchronize changes from the primary
options.D: Replace all write-ahead logging

questions.explanation: Replicas are synchronized read-serving nodes.

questions.question: A recommendation API has approximately 100 reads per write. What is the lecture’s proposed way to reduce primary load?

options.A: Execute all reads within a single write transaction.
options.B: Send all feature lookups to the primary.
options.C: Shard the schema into separate databases on the same server.
options.D: Distribute SELECT queries over multiple read replicas.

questions.explanation: Read-scale architecture distributes SELECT operations among replicas so the primary can focus on writes.

questions.question: Why are read replicas useful during model inference?

options.A: They guarantee that each feature vector is globally unique.
options.B: They can serve feature-vector retrieval requests.
options.C: They eliminate the need for all database indexes.
options.D: They automatically synchronize model weights.

questions.explanation: The AI inference use case in the slide fetches feature vectors through replicas.

questions.question: When does the primary acknowledge a commit under the synchronous replication model described in the slides?

options.A: Before producing any WAL records
options.B: Immediately after receiving a client query
options.C: After receiving the required replica confirmation
options.D: Only after every replica has been restarted

questions.explanation: Synchronous replication requires a replica acknowledgement before commit completion.

questions.question: What failure risk is highlighted for synchronous replication if the required replica is unavailable?

options.A: Writes may be blocked while the primary waits for confirmation.
options.B: Previously committed rows are automatically deleted.
options.C: The primary silently switches to sharding.
options.D: Read-only queries on the primary become illegal.

questions.explanation: The trade-off described is increased write latency and potential write unavailability.

questions.question: In asynchronous replication, what may happen before a replica receives the latest update?

options.A: The replica must reject every SELECT.
options.B: The primary waits for all replicas to confirm.
options.C: The cluster changes its sharding key.
options.D: The primary successfully commits locally.

questions.explanation: Asynchronous replication commits first and ships changes to replicas afterward.

questions.question: An asynchronous primary crashes just after committing, before sending its newest change. What risk follows?

options.A: The last commit must already be on all replicas.
options.B: The newest committed change may be missing from replicas.
options.D: The primary automatically rolls back all earlier commits.

questions.explanation: The slide identifies data-loss risk if the primary fails before propagation.

questions.question: A replica briefly returns an older customer balance while the primary has the new balance. Which replication trade-off does this show?

options.A: A local partitioning error
options.D: A guaranteed two-phase commit failure

questions.explanation: Asynchronous replicas can temporarily lag behind the primary.

questions.question: What is failover in a primary-replica cluster?

options.A: Promoting a replica to become the new writable primary
options.B: Moving every row to a newly selected shard
options.C: Increasing the RAM on the failed node
options.D: Restarting all nodes in a fixed round-robin order

questions.explanation: Failover replaces a failed primary by promoting a replica.

questions.question: Which sequence follows the failover workflow described in the slides?

options.A: Promotion → detection → election → reconfiguration
options.D: Detection → election → promotion → reconfiguration

questions.explanation: The four listed steps occur in that order.

questions.question: Which tools are explicitly mentioned as options for automating PostgreSQL failover?

options.A: pgAdmin and psql
options.D: HBase and CouchDB

questions.explanation: Patroni and Repmgr appear in the failover slide.

questions.question: For large AI training jobs, what deployment choice is recommended in the lecture?

options.A: Perform every bulk read against the writable primary.
options.C: Read large datasets from read replicas to reduce pressure on production.
options.D: Place all training features on a single unreplicated node.

questions.explanation: Training data can be read from replicas to avoid stressing the production primary.

questions.question: Why might a global inference service deploy replicas in multiple geographic regions?

options.A: To reduce data-access latency near users
options.B: To force all writes to cross every region
options.D: To make row identifiers sequential

questions.explanation: Geographic replication is used to reduce latency for local inference users.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes sharding from replication?

options.A: Sharding copies every row to every node; replication splits rows.
options.B: Both strategies necessarily keep identical data on every node.
options.C: Sharding affects only indexes, while replication affects tables.
options.D: Sharding distributes different subsets; replication maintains copies.

questions.explanation: Shards hold unique subsets of a logical dataset, unlike replicas that maintain copies.

questions.question: A dataset of ten billion rows is split into ten data subsets on different servers. Which concept best matches the lecture?

options.A: Synchronous replication
options.D: Materialized views

questions.explanation: The slide presents the ten-billion-row example as a use case for sharding.

questions.question: A table is divided into smaller tables, but all partitions remain in the same PostgreSQL instance. What is this called?

options.A: Local horizontal partitioning
options.D: Cross-region failover

questions.explanation: Local horizontal partitioning operates within one database instance; sharding distributes pieces across nodes.

questions.question: Compared with local horizontal partitioning, what capability is added by sharding?

options.A: Automatic foreign keys across all servers
options.C: Scaling CPU and RAM resources across multiple machines
options.D: A requirement that each server has identical rows

questions.explanation: Sharding can distribute work and data over multiple physical servers.

questions.question: What determines the destination shard for an individual record?

options.A: The newest available replica
options.D: The value and routing rule of the sharding key

questions.explanation: The sharding key is the column used to assign a row to a shard.

questions.question: New customer IDs grow sequentially, and the newest IDs always land on the last range shard. What risk is highlighted?

options.A: The last shard cannot store indexes.
options.B: That shard becomes a write hotspot.
options.C: All shards receive exactly the same load.
options.D: Every query automatically needs two-phase commit.

questions.explanation: Range-based sharding can concentrate new users on one shard.

questions.question: Which formula illustrates hash-based shard assignment in the slides?

options.A: hash(customer_id) % N
options.D: SUM(customer_id) OVER (PARTITION BY N)

questions.explanation: The slide uses hash(customer_id) modulo number of shards to distribute rows.

questions.question: Why is choosing the wrong sharding key expensive to correct later?

options.A: It forces synchronous replication forever.
options.B: It makes every index unusable by definition.
options.C: Changing placement may require resharding existing records.
options.D: It permanently disables failover.

questions.explanation: Correcting poor distribution can require a costly resharding process.

questions.question: Why should applications avoid frequent cross-shard joins when possible?

options.A: A join becomes a full database backup.
options.B: Cross-shard joins never return consistent rows.
options.C: SQL does not support JOIN syntax in distributed systems.
options.D: Combining data stored on different servers can be very slow.

questions.explanation: The slide identifies expensive cross-shard joins as an important complexity cost.

questions.question: Which integrity problem is identified when related tables reside on separate shards?

options.A: All local foreign keys stop working.
options.B: Cross-shard foreign keys are usually not enforced by the DBMS.
options.C: Every shard automatically gains duplicate primary keys.
options.D: Indexes cannot reference any local column.

questions.explanation: The lecture notes that foreign-key constraints across shards are generally unsupported.

questions.question: What is identified as a mechanism for coordinating ACID transactions spanning shards?

options.A: Two-phase commit
options.D: An HTTP cache

questions.explanation: The lecture cites two-phase commit for distributed transactions and highlights its performance cost.

questions.question: A social network stores each user’s profile and associated activity on the same shard. What is the intended advantage?

options.A: The primary never needs to commit writes.
options.B: All users necessarily share one global shard.
options.C: User-profile queries can access related data locally.
options.D: The system no longer requires authentication.

questions.explanation: Sharding by user_id co-locates a user’s data and speeds profile retrieval.

questions.question: Which AI-oriented dataset is explicitly cited as a candidate for sharding?

options.A: A single local configuration file
options.D: Billions of embeddings in a feature store

questions.explanation: Feature stores holding billions of vectors are a stated sharding example.

questions.question: According to the lecture, what is the key CAP trade-off when a network partition occurs?

options.A: Choose whether to keep ACID or SQL support.
options.D: Choose between vertical and horizontal scaling.

questions.explanation: The CAP constraint during partitions is the conflict between strong consistency and availability.

questions.question: Who is credited in the lecture with proposing the CAP theorem in 2000?

options.A: Eric Brewer
options.D: Michael Stonebraker

questions.explanation: The introduction credits Eric Brewer in 2000.

questions.question: Which outcome satisfies the lecture’s definition of strong consistency?

options.A: Every read gets an answer, but it may be arbitrarily old.
options.B: A read can return a newer value on one node and an older value on another.
options.C: Each read returns the latest write or an error.
options.D: Every write is acknowledged before any node stores it.

questions.explanation: Strong consistency is defined as receiving the most recent write or an error.

questions.question: After a bank withdrawal is committed, a remote read is required to reflect the new balance or fail. Which CAP property is prioritized?

options.A: Availability
options.D: Consistency

questions.explanation: The bank-account analogy illustrates strong consistency across nodes.

questions.question: Which behavior is consistent with the lecture’s definition of availability?

options.A: Every request gets a non-error response, potentially with stale data.
options.B: Every response must contain the most recent value.
options.C: The service may reject requests until all nodes synchronize.
options.D: All nodes must commit the same write simultaneously.

questions.explanation: Availability emphasizes a response to every request, even when replicas are out of sync.

questions.question: A feed still opens during a partition but shows an older Like count. Which guarantee is being favored?

options.A: Strong consistency
options.D: Zero-lag replication

questions.explanation: The slide’s social-feed analogy shows an available but potentially stale response.

questions.question: What does partition tolerance mean in the CAP theorem as defined in the slides?

options.A: All servers must store unique subsets of rows.
options.B: The database cannot operate without a primary.
options.C: The system continues operating despite dropped or delayed messages between nodes.
options.D: Network latency is guaranteed to be zero.

questions.explanation: Partition tolerance concerns continued operation when communication between nodes is disrupted.

questions.question: Why does the lecture treat partition tolerance as effectively mandatory for distributed systems?

options.A: It improves the speed of every SQL join.
options.C: It is a setting that users can turn off.
options.D: Real networks can fail or split unexpectedly.

questions.explanation: Partitions are treated as unavoidable network faults in real deployments.

questions.question: A partition separates two replicas. One side rejects requests rather than risk serving inconsistent data. Which design priority does this best represent?

options.A: CP
options.D: Pure read scaling

questions.explanation: In the lecture, CP preserves consistency during partitions by sacrificing availability for some requests.

questions.question: During a network partition, both sides continue responding even though values may disagree. Which design priority is illustrated?

options.A: Synchronous replication only
options.D: Serializable execution

questions.explanation: AP maintains non-error responses but permits temporary inconsistency.

questions.question: Which application is placed under CP use cases in the lecture?

options.A: A social-media Like counter
options.D: A feed of noncritical recommendations

questions.explanation: Banking, stock trading and medical records are examples in the CP column.

questions.question: Which application is listed as an AP-oriented use case?

options.A: Bank balance transfers
options.D: Video comments and caching

questions.explanation: YouTube comments, Facebook feeds, and caches appear under AP.

questions.question: How is single-node PostgreSQL characterized in the lecture’s CAP mapping table?

options.A: A CA-oriented relational system
options.C: A CP system that never allows reads
options.D: A sharded NoSQL system

questions.explanation: The table labels PostgreSQL (Single Node) as CA / Pure ACID; this is a lecture classification of a non-distributed setup.

questions.question: Which pair is placed in the AP category in the lecture’s database comparison?

options.A: PostgreSQL and HBase
options.D: Redis and HBase

questions.explanation: The CAP-mapping table lists Cassandra and CouchDB under AP.

questions.question: What qualification does the lecture provide about mapping database products to CAP categories?

options.A: Every product permanently belongs to a single CAP class.
options.B: CAP classification depends exclusively on SQL syntax.
options.C: Configurations such as PostgreSQL replication can shift the consistency/availability trade-off.
options.D: Replication settings never influence distributed behavior.

questions.explanation: The slide notes that databases with replication can be tuned toward CP or AP depending on configuration.

questions.question: In the dvdrental Docker lab, which port is assigned to the read-only replica?
questions.explanation: The lab assigns port 5432 to the primary and 5433 to the replica.

questions.question: Which component is used to start the preconfigured primary-replica environment?

options.A: A Docker Compose configuration
options.D: A standalone machine-learning notebook

questions.explanation: The lab uses Docker Compose to start nodes with streaming replication.

questions.question: Where does the lab direct students to restore the dvdrental sample database?

options.A: The replica before the primary
options.D: The Docker host outside PostgreSQL

questions.explanation: The specified restore command targets the primary database.

questions.question: Which PostgreSQL configuration setting enables the WAL information needed for replica streaming in the lecture?

options.A: archive_mode = off
options.D: default_transaction_read_only = off

questions.explanation: The primary postgresql.conf slide explicitly sets wal_level = replica.

questions.question: What is the role of max_wal_senders = 10 in the lecture’s primary configuration?

options.A: Limit SQL query results to ten rows
options.D: Configure capacity for WAL-sending processes

questions.explanation: max_wal_senders controls how many WAL sender processes may run.

questions.question: Which file contains the lab’s network authentication entry for a replication user?

options.A: pg_hba.conf
options.D: pg_indexes

questions.explanation: The slide places host replication replicator ... md5 in pg_hba.conf.

questions.question: How does the replica obtain changes from the primary in the lab’s streaming setup?

options.A: By periodically copying query screenshots
options.B: By receiving and replaying streamed WAL records
options.D: By rebuilding all tables from CSV per request

questions.explanation: The primary streams WAL, which is replayed at the replica.

questions.question: After updating customer.active on the primary, what is the intended verification on the replica?

options.A: Run pg_restore again before every read.
options.B: Change the replica into a writable shard.
options.C: Query the same customer and observe the propagated value.
options.D: Delete the customer so both nodes match.

questions.explanation: The lab checks that the new active value can be read on the replica after replication.

questions.question: Why should DELETE FROM rental fail when executed on the read-only replica in the lab?

options.A: The rental table has no primary key.
options.B: Only SELECT queries can be parameterized.
options.D: The replica rejects writes in a read-only transaction.

questions.explanation: The lab shows a cannot execute DELETE in a read-only transaction error.

questions.question: A project requires low write latency even if a replica is temporarily behind. Which option matches the lecture’s trade-off?

options.A: Asynchronous replication, accepting possible lag
options.B: Synchronous replication, waiting for replica acknowledgement
options.C: A single-node setup with no redundancy
options.D: Two-phase commit over all read replicas

questions.explanation: Asynchronous mode favors fast commits but admits replication lag; synchronous waits for acknowledgement.

questions.question: An application suffers uneven shard load because new IDs all fall into the highest range. Which alternative does the slide present for more even distribution?

options.A: Replacing all replicas with one server
options.D: Enabling synchronous replication everywhere

questions.explanation: Hash-based sharding is presented as a way to distribute keys more evenly than ranges.

questions.question: Which statement avoids a common misunderstanding of the CAP theorem?

options.A: Every distributed system always chooses exactly two properties regardless of failures.
options.B: A non-partitioned system must reject either all reads or all writes.
options.C: When a partition occurs, maintaining strong consistency can require rejecting some requests.
options.D: Partition tolerance means the network will never lose messages.

questions.explanation: The lecture specifically frames the C-versus-A choice in the presence of a network partition.
